lesson.title: Unplugged, then plugged
lesson.subtitle: Real ideas with cards and chalk

video.title: Unplugged, then plugged: Real ideas with cards and chalk
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah — education lecturer, Bangladesh (main character)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Our school has six tablets for nine hundred pupils. Some colleagues say: then we can’t teach computing. But the big ideas of computing need no device at all.
Today: unplugged lessons that teach real computing, and how to connect them to code.

Unplugged means teaching computing ideas with cards, string, chalk and people. CS Unplugged, a free collection from New Zealand, has dozens of activities. Sorting networks, binary cards, searching games, and error-detecting card tricks.

Here’s a favourite. Five pupils hold cards with one, two, four, eight and sixteen dots. Each card is face up or face down: on or off, one or zero. To make thirteen, show eight, four and one. Five cards make every number up to thirty-one.

Unplugged works best when it’s linked to code soon after. After the binary cards, show Python doing the same thing. bin of thirteen gives one, one, zero, one. The idea came first; now pupils see a computer do it.

Unplugged has limits. It teaches concepts, but not the habits of writing and debugging real code. Research suggests it works best as a start, not instead of programming. So plan the plugged part, even with one phone for the class.
Quick check! Which of these teaches a computing idea with no device: pupils sorting themselves by height in a chalk sorting network, or watching a video about computers?
The sorting network. Pupils walk along chalk lines, compare numbers at each meeting point, and swap if needed. They’re acting out a real algorithm, and they can feel why it works.

Choose activities by the idea they teach, not by how fun they look. Human robot for algorithms. Binary cards for data. Guess my number for searching. A card trick for detecting errors. Each one needs only paper, chalk or cards.
A good unplugged lesson has a shape. Start with a puzzle. Let pupils act it out. Name the idea: this is binary, this is an algorithm. Then show it in code, on one phone if that’s all you have.
In the app, open Bits and bytes. Flip eight switches to make any number from zero to two hundred and fifty-five, then make sixty-five and see the letter A. It’s the binary cards, plugged in.
Your turn. Your class has just played the binary cards game. What’s the best next step?

scenes.on_screen_text: Real ideas · choose well · shape · a start
scenes.narration: Link it to code. Remember: unplugged teaches real ideas with cards, chalk and people. Choose activities by the idea they teach. Give each lesson a shape: puzzle, act it out, name it, code it. And it’s a start, not a replacement.
Try it in class tomorrow: binary cards. Make five cards with one, two, four, eight and sixteen dots. Five pupils show numbers the class calls out. End by showing bin of a number on your phone.

options.text: Pupils sorting themselves in a chalk sorting network
Copying a program from the board

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — pupils act out a real algorithm: comparing and swapping.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a video or copying isn’t doing the idea. In the sorting network, pupils act out an algorithm.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — unplugged works best when it’s connected to code soon after.
